problems.source_says: The main PDF establishes that six trained evaluators rated the emails, but does not identify the Study 2 evaluators as lay raters or crowd workers. It refers to SI B4.1 for their demographics and notes that evaluators differed in industry backgrounds and education. Codebook section 6 defines human_raters specifically as lay raters or crowd workers and expert_raters as domain experts, instructors, or professionals. The form itself says professional qualifications cannot be established, which does not establish lay status. Thus this categorical value is unsupported for all four rated outcomes; the appropriate category remains unconfirmed and should be null pending the evaluator information. This finding does not establish expert_raters as the replacement.
problems.quote: To evaluate email quality, six evaluators were trained to rate the quality of the emails along the same four dimensions as in Study 1 (i.e., Completeness, Relevance, Actionability, Creativity).
problems.locator: Main PDF p. 2, Research motivation and overview (SI B3.1/B4.1 reference) and Methods, Study 2 paragraph; p. 9, Limitations, evaluator-background discussion; creativity-codebook.md section 6, Measure. SI B4.1 is not in the saved PDF.

confirmed.statement: S2-O1 through S2-O4 are evaluator ratings of participants’ produced emails, not participant self-reports; the explicit Creativity rating satisfies criterion 3.
confirmed.locator: Main PDF p. 2, Methods, Study 2 paragraph; p. 3, opening rubric paragraph and Statistical analysis.

confirmed.statement: For all five outcomes, AI-generated recommendations were supplied directly below the task instructions during email production; controls wrote without AI content. ai_available_when_produced=yes, timing=immediate, and question=with_ai are supported; there is no post-removal assessment.
confirmed.locator: Main PDF p. 2, Research motivation and overview and Methods; p. 9, Limitations, first paragraph; codebook sections 1 and 6.

confirmed.statement: S2-O1 is an overall Creativity rating, S2-O2 measures information and explanatory detail (elaboration), and S2-O3/S2-O4 measure topical relevance and actionable solutions (usefulness). None measures similarity across different people or categories within one person.
confirmed.locator: Main PDF p. 3, opening rubric paragraph; codebook section 6, Construct.

confirmed.statement: S2-O5 is computed length of the produced email in normalized characters, supporting scored_on_output=true, construct=elaboration, and unit=output. The codebook has no direct character-count measure category, so its null measure avoids an unsupported mapping.
confirmed.locator: Main PDF p. 6, AI effects on productivity across languages; p. 3, Statistical analysis; codebook section 6, Construct, Measure, and Unit.

confirmed.statement: The main PDF defines the quality response as the rating of email i and clusters standard errors by participant, but does not state whether the analysis uses individual evaluator ratings or averaged email ratings. The null unit and n_units for S2-O1 through S2-O4 appropriately leave that distinction unresolved.
confirmed.locator: Main PDF p. 3, Statistical analysis, equations (1) and (2) and surrounding text; p. 4, evaluator-pair reliability discussion; SI Table S5 is referenced but absent.

confirmed.statement: The four rated dimensions are explicitly called the primary outcome variables; length is an additional productivity outcome, supporting their paper_primary versus secondary coding.
confirmed.locator: Main PDF p. 3, Statistical analysis, first paragraph.

confirmed.statement: S2-O1 reports the exact Chinese-versus-English creativity interaction: 0.49 standard deviations less Creativity, p=0.016. The form correctly treats this as a difference between language-specific AI effects.
confirmed.locator: Main PDF p. 3, AI effects on the quality of human work across languages, final paragraph; Statistical analysis, equation (2).

confirmed.statement: S2-O4 reports the exact actionability interactions: Arabic versus English, 0.59 standard deviations less improvement, p=0.015; Chinese versus English, 0.47 standard deviations less improvement, p=0.022.
confirmed.locator: Main PDF p. 3, AI effects on the quality of human work across languages, final paragraph; Statistical analysis, equation (2).

confirmed.statement: Figure 1 supports S2-O1’s higher treated-group creativity medians in all three languages and S2-O4’s higher actionability medians in English and Chinese with equal Arabic medians. The plots use a 1–5 scale; these are descriptive directions, not significance tests.
confirmed.locator: Main PDF p. 5, Figure 1(c) and 1(d), visually inspected from an in-memory PDF rendering; p. 4, Figure 1 caption.

confirmed.statement: S2-O2 and S2-O3 accurately quote similar improvements in completeness and relevance across languages. Figure 1(a)/(b) is consistent with higher treated-group medians; the main PDF supplies no numerical treatment estimates for these dimensions.
confirmed.locator: Main PDF p. 3, Study 2 quality results; p. 4, Figure 1(a)/(b), visually inspected from an in-memory PDF rendering.

confirmed.statement: All S2-O5 reported numbers match: English 49%, 631 normalized characters, p=0.000; Arabic 25%, 283, p=0.010; Chinese 46%, 532, p=0.000; English-versus-Arabic difference p=0.034. The p=0.000 values reproduce the paper’s displayed precision.
confirmed.locator: Main PDF p. 6, AI effects on productivity across languages, first paragraph, referring to SI Figure S4/Table S9.

confirmed.statement: The task-type results retained in measure_detail match the printed p-values: Arabic actionability 0.053, Chinese creativity 0.025, and Arabic/Chinese length 0.037/0.020. Figures 2 and 3 concern the same actionability and creativity outcomes, not additional constructs.
confirmed.locator: Main PDF p. 6, Task types, referring to SI Table S13; p. 7, Figure 2 caption; p. 8, Figure 3 caption.

confirmed.statement: No additional qualifying participant-output creativity or diversity outcome was identified in the complete saved document. Confidence and perceived difficulty are self-reported, writing time is a process measure, and Study 1 rates AI-generated content without human production. References to BLEU, ROUGE, and BERTScore describe prior literature.

Evaluator backgrounds, rating aggregation, supplementary regression tables, and any supplement-only outcomes could not be independently checked: Python urllib requests to both the Europe PMC full-text API and PMC Open Access API failed with WinError 10013; no supplementary values were inferred.

summary: Criterion 3 holds because trained evaluators scored creativity on participants’ business emails produced with supplied AI content or without it. The blanket coding conclusion is refuted because human_raters denotes lay raters or crowd workers in the codebook, while the available PDF does not establish that status for any of the four rated outcomes; the recorded numerical results match the main PDF.
